problem: Existing reviews of embodied navigation rarely focus on how LLMs are used for navigation, nor compare LLM-based with non-LLM navigation models and the datasets used. The field lacks a taxonomy of LLM roles in navigation and a consolidated view of their strengths and weaknesses.
motivation: LLMs offer few-shot planning, commonsense reasoning and language grounding that could help agents navigate unfamiliar environments, but they face problems with multimodal fusion, latency, spatial reasoning and training efficiency. A structured survey helps researchers select methods and datasets and identify open challenges.
key_idea: Categorize LLM-based navigation works into two roles, planners that generate actions and semantic-understanding providers that extract goal-relevant information, and compare them with non-LLM models, datasets and metrics.
insight: The survey concludes that LLM navigation agents mostly rely on frozen pre-trained LLMs without task-specific fine-tuning, which limits fine-grained instruction following, spatial reasoning and long-horizon planning. It notes that information loss when converting visual observations to text (e.g., NavGPT) is a bottleneck, motivating multimodal LLM inputs. No ablations are performed; the performance tables are compiled from the original papers and are not directly comparable across benchmarks.
method: Taxonomy: splits LLM navigation into 'Planning' (CLIP-Nav, NavGPT, VELMA, MiC, SayNav) and 'Semantic Understanding' (LM-Nav, BEVBert, ESC, SQA3D), with diagrams in Figs 2-5.
Method review: describes each LLM-based work (LM-Nav, CLIP-Nav, SQA3D, ESC, NavGPT, VELMA, MiC, SayNav, ETPNav) in terms of its architecture and role of the LLM.
Non-LLM comparison: covers CoW, ZSON, VLMap, OVRL-V2 and traditional planners (Theta*, LPA*, MAPF), contrasting adaptability, compute and data needs.
Metrics and results table: defines PL, NE, OSR, SR, SPL, CLS, nDTW/SDTW and compiles reported SR/SPL from papers on Habitat, RoboTHOR, Gibson, HM3D, MP3D, REVERIE, R2R (Tables IV-V).
Dataset analysis: compares MP3D, Touchdown, R2R, CVDN, REVERIE, RxR, SOON, ProcTHOR, R3ED, X-Embodiment (Table VI).
Challenges and future directions: dynamic path optimization, task-specific LLM architecture optimization, integration with autonomous driving, multimodal fusion, privacy.
numbers_note: Survey paper; no own method results. Tables IV and V only compile results of other methods taken from their original papers, so none are reported.
results: As a survey, it has no new experimental results. It compiles reported numbers, e.g., BEVBert reaches 64% SPL / 75% SR on R2R and SayNav 34% SPL / 60.32% SR on HM3D, and concludes LLM navigators offer adaptability and language interaction but need heavy compute and data.
limitations: Performance tables are copied from original papers with different setups and are not comparable; many entries are missing.
Coverage is limited (about a dozen methods) and several described works (e.g., BEVBert, ETPNav, OVRL) are not LLM-based, blurring the LLM taxonomy.
Analysis is largely descriptive with few quantitative conclusions.
